title: Open Source: Contributors, Institutions and the Software Supply Chain

paras: Open-source software is a governance and production model that underpins the Internet, operating systems, programming languages, cloud infrastructure, databases, browsers, cybersecurity and AI tooling. Its success depends on maintainers, review, licensing, sustainable funding and deployment operators—not just public code repositories.

Collaborative software exchange predates the modern open-source label. Richard Stallman's GNU project (announced 1983) and the Free Software Foundation (1985) advanced software freedom and copyleft licensing. BSD UNIX traditions contributed networking and operating-system components. Linus Torvalds initiated the Linux kernel in 1991; GNU utilities and numerous independent projects helped form complete Linux-based operating environments. The Open Source Initiative formed in 1998 to promote a defined open-source licensing model.

Tim Berners-Lee and CERN made foundational Web technology broadly available; the IETF's open RFC process and W3C standards enabled interoperability. The Apache Software Foundation, Mozilla, Eclipse Foundation, Linux Foundation and Cloud Native Computing Foundation became important institutional homes for collaborative projects. Standards development and open-source implementation are related but different activities.

Contributors include individual volunteers, academic laboratories, corporate engineers, public-sector teams, nonprofits and foundation employees. Firms may fund projects because shared infrastructure reduces duplication, expands ecosystems, attracts developers or supports commercial services. Revenue can come from enterprise support, managed hosting, subscriptions, consulting, proprietary add-ons and hardware.

Open source does not automatically mean free hosting, unrestricted trademarks, absence of copyright, verified security or guaranteed maintenance. Licensing obligations, export restrictions, dependency provenance, vulnerability management and contributor governance matter in production.

blocks.h2: How an open-source component reaches a bank or telecom network
paras: A bank may run Linux on virtual machines, PostgreSQL for selected applications, OpenTelemetry for tracing and Kubernetes for orchestration, while using proprietary core-banking software and regulated payment networks. A telecom operator may run open-source network functions on commercial hardware, subject to interoperability, security and operational requirements. Open and proprietary components coexist.

Software bills of materials (SBOMs), reproducible builds, signed releases, dependency scanning, code review, least-privilege access and incident response are relevant to open-source supply-chain governance. An open repository provides inspectability, not automatic proof of safety. Procurement decisions should assess maintainer health, licenses, patch cadence and operational support.
